trial_name: FACTT — Conservative vs Liberal Fluid Management in Acute Lung Injury (2006)
citation: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) Clinical Trials Network. Comparison of two fluid-management strategies in acute lung injury. N Engl J Med. 2006;354(24):2564-2575.
one_liner: In established ALI/ARDS, a conservative fluid strategy did not reduce 60-day mortality but improved ventilator-free and ICU-free days compared to a liberal strategy.

pico.population: Mechanically ventilated ICU patients with ALI/ARDS (PaO2:FiO2 ≤300, bilateral infiltrates, no left atrial hypertension) within 48 hours of meeting criteria.
pico.intervention: Conservative fluid-management strategy targeting lower filling pressures (CVP <4 mm Hg or PAOP <8 mm Hg) via a 7-day protocolised algorithm.
pico.comparison: Liberal fluid-management strategy targeting higher filling pressures (CVP 10–14 mm Hg or PAOP 14–18 mm Hg) via the same 7-day protocolised algorithm.
pico.outcome: Primary: death before discharge home by day 60. Key secondary: ventilator-free days and ICU-free days to day 28.

background.existing_knowledge: ALI/ARDS is characterised by increased alveolar-capillary permeability; hydrostatic pressure and total fluid balance can modulate oedema burden and gas exchange. Clinical practice historically oscillated between haemodynamic support (liberal fluids) and lung protection (fluid restriction/diuresis).
background.knowledge_gap: A large, protocolised randomised trial was lacking to determine if a conservative fluid strategy could improve outcomes without causing shock or renal injury.
background.hypothesis: In adults with ALI, a conservative fluid-management strategy reduces death before discharge home by day 60 and improves clinical recovery (ventilator-free days) compared with a liberal strategy.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre (20 North American centres), investigator-initiated NIH/ARDSNet trial; factorial design with simultaneous randomisation to haemodynamic catheter (pulmonary-artery vs central venous) and to fluid-management strategy; open-label protocolised intervention.
methods.setting: Mechanically ventilated ICU patients with ALI/ARDS managed within ARDSNet protocols. Enrolled June 2000 to October 2005.

inclusion: Bilateral infiltrates consistent with pulmonary oedema
No evidence of left atrial hypertension (or, if measured, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure ≤18 mm Hg)
Randomisation within 48 hours after ALI criteria first met
Catheter inserted within 4 hours of randomisation
First fluid-management protocol instruction within 2 hours after catheter placement
exclusion: Inability/unwillingness to pursue full aggressive care

methods.intervention: Conservative fluid-management strategy (7-day protocol): target lower intravascular filling pressures (CVP <4 mm Hg if central venous catheter; PAOP <8 mm Hg if pulmonary-artery catheter). Protocol-directed 4-hourly reassessments using a decision support algorithm incorporating intravascular pressure, evidence of shock, and evidence of ineffective circulation. Typical actions when haemodynamically suitable: fluid restriction and diuresis (e.g., furosemide).
methods.comparison: Liberal fluid-management strategy (7-day protocol): target higher intravascular filling pressures (CVP 10–14 mm Hg if central venous catheter; PAOP 14–18 mm Hg if pulmonary-artery catheter). Same structured 4-hourly reassessment framework, with protocol actions favouring fluid administration and reduced diuresis.
methods.blinding: Unblinded. Primary endpoint (death before discharge home by day 60) is objective. Secondary endpoints (ventilator-/ICU-free days) are partially care-process dependent but were assessed within an ARDSNet protocol environment.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 1000 patients to provide 90% power (two-sided α=0.05) to detect a 10 percentage-point absolute reduction in the primary endpoint (from 31% to 21%).
methods.primary_outcome: Death before discharge home by day 60.
methods.follow_up: Outcomes assessed through day 60 for mortality/discharge home status and dialysis; ventilator-free/ICU-free days assessed to day 28; protocol intervention applied for 7 days after randomisation.

headline_bullets: 60-day mortality was similar between groups (25.5% conservative vs 28.4% liberal; P=0.30).
Conservative strategy improved ventilator-free days (14.6 vs 12.1; P<0.001) and ICU-free days (13.4 vs 11.2; P<0.001).
A large separation in cumulative fluid balance was achieved at day 7 (−136 mL vs +6992 mL; P<0.001).
Dialysis use was not significantly increased (10% vs 14%; P=0.06), but electrolyte imbalances were more common (42% vs 19%; P=0.001).

outcomes_table.outcome: Days with dialysis to day 60 (among dialysed)

outcomes_table.note: Defined as any of: potassium ≤3.0 mmol/L (26% vs 22%), sodium ≥150 mmol/L (25% vs 18%), bicarbonate >40 mmol/L (6% vs 2%)

subgroup_table.note: No significant interaction between the catheter intervention and fluid strategy.
No significant interaction between baseline shock status and fluid strategy with respect to primary/major secondary outcomes.

safety: Electrolyte imbalance events were more frequent with conservative management (42% vs 19%; P=0.001).
Serious adverse events were uncommon in both groups (3% vs 1%; P=0.21).

domains.notes: Centralised computer-generated randomisation with permuted blocks; factorial design; allocation concealment supported by automated assignment.
Open-label delivery; primary outcome objective; secondary outcomes (ventilator-/ICU-free days) potentially influenced by care processes, mitigated by protocolised ARDSNet management environment.

1001 randomised; 1 patient in the liberal group withdrew consent before receiving the intervention and was excluded from analysis; analysed cohorts were 503 (conservative) and 497 (liberal); mortality follow-up to day 60 was otherwise complete.

Large between-group separation achieved in fluid balance: cumulative day-7 balance −136 ± 491 mL (conservative) vs 6992 ± 502 mL (liberal). Higher furosemide dosing in conservative group on each study day (e.g., day 1: 148.94 ± 8.52 mg/24h vs 74.27 ± 7.48 mg/24h).

Groups were well balanced across major prognostic factors (e.g., APACHE III score 93.1 ± 1.4 vs 95.2 ± 1.4; shock criteria at baseline 33% vs 36%; PaO2:FiO2 179.8 ± 4.1 vs 176.7 ± 4.2). Prerandomisation fluid balance was already positive (e.g., 2655 ± 156 mL vs 2875 ± 166 mL).

internal_validity.verdict: Strong overall: randomisation and follow-up were robust, protocol separation in fluid balance was large and sustained, and the primary outcome was objective, although open-label delivery could influence process-dependent secondary endpoints.

domains.notes: Adults with ALI in academic/tertiary ICUs within a North American clinical trials network; exclusion criteria removed patients with advanced chronic organ disease and those not committed to full support.

The intervention relied on frequent reassessment and haemodynamic targets (CVP or PAOP), which may not reflect contemporary practice where pulmonary-artery catheters are uncommon and dynamic assessments are favoured. Findings most directly apply after initial stabilisation/resuscitation in established ALI/ARDS, rather than the earliest shock-resuscitation phase. Protocolised strategies are feasible in well-resourced ICUs; implementation in resource-limited settings may be constrained.

external_validity.verdict: Moderately strong for protocol-capable ICUs managing established ALI/ARDS, but less directly transferable to settings without structured haemodynamic monitoring workflows or to the earliest resuscitation phase of shock.

strengths: Protocolised and clearly differentiated fluid strategies
Clinically meaningful secondary outcomes (ventilator-free and ICU-free days)
Factorial design permitted assessment of catheter–strategy interaction
limitations: Reliance on filling-pressure targets (CVP/PAOP) and intensive protocol infrastructure
Prerandomisation fluid exposure substantial (positive balance at baseline)
Mortality endpoint potentially insensitive to smaller effect sizes
Interpretation of renal function complicated by haemoconcentration during conservative management

critical_appraisal.summary: A well-conducted, large RCT with robust protocol separation showing that a conservative fluid strategy in established ALI/ARDS improves respiratory recovery without a mortality benefit, though open-label design and reliance on pressure-based targets limit generalisability to modern, less invasive monitoring settings.
strengths: Large sample size with high follow-up completeness
Significant and sustained separation in the intervention (fluid balance)
weaknesses: Open-label design may bias process-of-care secondary outcomes
Use of CVP/PAOP targets is less common in contemporary practice
Mortality benefit may have been missed due to power assumptions

sections.authors_conclusion: A conservative strategy of fluid management in patients with acute lung injury improved lung function and shortened the duration of mechanical ventilation and intensive care without increasing nonpulmonary organ failures.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: In established ALI/ARDS, after initial haemodynamic stabilisation, a conservative fluid strategy should be used to increase ventilator-free days, though it does not reduce mortality.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Patients with established ALI/ARDS in protocol-capable ICUs, after the initial shock-resuscitation phase.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Fluid restriction should be applied during the active resuscitation phase of shock.
implementation_caveats: Requires careful monitoring for electrolyte and acid-base disturbances.
Interpret serum creatinine changes in the context of haemoconcentration from diuresis.
The original protocol used CVP/PAOP targets; a simplified conservative protocol may be more feasible.

controversies.notes: The trial tested a protocol applied after ALI was established (often following substantial prerandomisation fluids), and contemporaneous commentary emphasised the distinction between early resuscitation and later conservative/deresuscitative phases rather than a single 'always restrictive' rule.

Conservative strategy produced haemoconcentration (higher creatinine/BUN over time), raising debate about whether 'renal safety' is best judged by dialysis alone versus creatinine-based AKI definitions that are sensitive to fluid balance; a later analysis demonstrated that adjusting creatinine for fluid accumulation materially alters AKI classification and its relationship with outcomes in ALI cohorts.

The original FACTT algorithm required frequent reassessment and catheter-derived targets; a simplified conservative protocol has been evaluated to improve feasibility while maintaining a conservative approach in ARDS care pathways.

FACTT was powered for a 10% absolute mortality reduction (31% to 21%); the observed mortality difference between strategies was smaller, so absence of statistical significance does not exclude more modest mortality effects.

Subsequent reviews and guidance documents commonly incorporate FACTT by supporting conservative fluid management after haemodynamic stabilisation in ARDS, while emphasising careful monitoring for electrolyte/acid–base derangements and renal effects (where definitions may be fluid-sensitive).

unresolved_questions: What is the optimal timing to transition from a liberal/resuscitative to a conservative/deresuscitative fluid strategy?
Can a simplified, non-catheter-based conservative fluid protocol achieve similar outcomes?
What is the true effect of conservative fluid management on renal function when using fluid-adjusted creatinine definitions?

numbers_to_remember: Day-7 fluid balance: −136 mL vs +6992 mL
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: After initial shock resuscitation in ARDS, switch to a conservative fluid strategy to get patients off the ventilator faster, but don't expect a mortality benefit.
